source.title: On Power Laws in Deep Ensembles
source.authors: E. Lobacheva; Nadezhda Chirkova; M. Kodryan; D. Vetrov

record.tranche_reason: The study tests when power-law fits describe calibrated loss in image-classification networks and reports conditions where calibration choices and network settings affect the fit or produce non-power-law behavior. This refines the scope of the claim, but it does not test language-model pretraining scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper reports image-classification results, not language-model pretraining results. Its cited language-model scaling findings are not recorded as rows. Detailed per-width and per-temperature fit traces are summarized below where the paper gives an explicit aggregate statement; other individual plotted fit parameters are left out.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to test classification NLL/CNLL of CNNs on CIFAR-10/100 against single-network parameter count and total parameter budget. That is a new modality (image classification) bearing on V5. It also shows whether a power law fits depends on calibration and regularization, which bears on V7. Most of the paper scales ensemble size n, a different axis from model, data or compute scale. Those results are recorded under fits_no_version. T3 fits better than T5: the paper extends the form to images rather than arguing a version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. With temperature applied before averaging, CNLL follows a power law in ensemble size from n = 1, with exponent slightly above the theoretical -1. Single-network CNLL follows a power law in size with exponent near -0.5, while non-calibrated NLL shows double descent. CNLL also follows a power law in total parameter budget. The optimal memory split usually has many more than one network and can be predicted from the fitted laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains convolutional image-classification networks and measures calibrated or non-calibrated classification NLL, rather than measuring held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy across model, token, and compute scales.
record.method_sensitivity: Calibration order (temperature before versus after averaging), temperature, regularization, dataset, architecture, network size, and ensemble size affect curve behavior or fitted parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Calibrated and fixed-temperature NLL of deep ensembles follow a power law in ensemble size n from n = 1. Exponent is slightly above -1 (e.g. -0.74 VGG CIFAR-100; -0.82 ResNet50 ImageNet).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ensemble loss falls as a power law in the number of ensemble members.

fits_no_version.finding: With temperature applied after averaging, NLL rises with n at high temperature, and CNLL can be non-convex for small unregularized networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ensemble-size power laws depend on the calibration procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: Power laws fitted on n = 1–4 predict large-ensemble CNLL with error 1–2 orders below CNLL, and predict optimal memory splits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ensemble-size power laws extrapolate to larger ensembles.

record.problems: The experiments concern image classification rather than language-model pretraining. Some power-law evidence is summarized qualitatively or displayed in figures; many fitted parameters vary across settings. The authors note possible under-regularization and reduced diversity as explanations for non-monotonic results, and say further investigation is needed.
record.rows_left_out: Individual fitted parameter values and RMSEs across every width, temperature, and dataset–architecture pairing are not separately listed; the text summarizes the broad results and the main named examples are recorded above. Further traces and supplementary sweeps appear in Figures 2–3, 10, 13, 15, 17, and 19–20.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation in model, data or compute scale. The only extrapolation is along ensemble size.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The memory-split optimum is a different allocation problem.
Depth, width or shape at fixed parameter count. Only width is varied, to change size.
Data or compute scaling, video, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer. Single-model size range spans only about 2.5 orders of magnitude (1/32 to 8 standard budgets).
Downstream task predictability from scale or loss.
Disagreement between published language-model laws; effects of parameter counting, schedule or fitting method.

missing.what: Non-monotonic ensemble NLL/CNLL vs member size for WideResNet CIFAR-100 (n=10), VGG CIFAR-10 (n=10) and WideResNet CIFAR-10 (n=4)
Power-law prediction of large-ensemble CNLL from n = 1..4 (ensemble axis, not model scale)

record.verdict_notes: Image classification on CIFAR and ImageNet, not language modelling. The single-model size sweep is narrow (about 2.5 orders of magnitude) and is the only part that bears on model-scale power laws. The record's V5 'supports' label wrongly included ensemble-size rows. The V7 link rests on calibration and regularization choices rather than on language-model fitting choices.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models as a function of parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to substantially larger language-model runs.

Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and the relative growth of parameters and tokens with compute. The paper studies parameter-count memory budgets, not compute-optimal language-model training.
Comparisons of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, and whether the same results hold for language-model pretraining loss. The experiments use image classification and calibrated or non-calibrated classification NLL.
Downstream language-model task performance and its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

Whether published language-model scaling laws disagree because of their counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices. The paper instead demonstrates fitting and curve-shape dependence in image-classification ensembles.
